http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/25/new-e.text: A federal judge has postponed a trial in the US of a former Libyan intelligence official charged in the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103, citing the discovery of new evidence that defence attorneys want to examine in the nearly 40-year-old case.Jury selection was scheduled to begin on Wednesday for the federal trial of Abu Agila Mohammd Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi in Washington. His trial will be the first in the US for the 21 December 1988 bombing over Lockerbie in Scotland, which killed 270 people.US District Judge Dabney Friedrich’s order didn’t specify the nature of the newly discovered evidence.Al-Marimi’s lawyers say prosecutors disclosed the new evidence to them on Saturday and added that their “constitutional and ethical obligations require the defence to investigate this development.”Defence attorney Laura Koenig, an assistant federal public defender, declined to elaborate in response to press inquiries.The judge scheduled a 1 September hearing in Washington to discuss the status of the case. Friedrich's brief order cited the complex nature of the case, the newly discovered evidence and “the need for the defence to determine how best to defend this case” as reasons to postpone the trial.Al-Marimi is charged in the US with making the bomb that downed the airplane.Flight 103 was 9.45 kilometres over Lockerbie when a bomb in the plane’s forward cargo area exploded 38 minutes after take-off from London Heathrow Airport.The flight was bound for John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York.The blast killed all 259 passengers and crew members and 11 people on the ground in Lockerbie, where the wreckage destroyed an entire block.Citizens of 21 countries were killed, including 190 Americans and 43 from the United Kingdom. The passengers included 35 Syracuse University students returning home from a semester abroad.Kara Weipz, board president of the nonprofit Victims of Pan Am Flight 103, said her organisation had received no details about the new evidence that prompted the trial delay. Weipz’s brother Richard Monetti was among the Syracuse students killed.She called the delay a shock and noted that some victims' relatives were already packing to head to the trial.“At the same time, for almost 38 years we've been seeking the truth of what happened,” Weipz said. “If that's what this is, then that's a good thing, and this delay is worth it. It's important to hear all the facts.”Prosecutors allege Al-Marimi and others carried out the bombing at the direction of Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, who was ousted and killed during a 2011 civil war.Two other Libyan intelligence agents were tried by a panel of Scottish judges on a former US military base in the Netherlands in 2000. The tribunal convicted one official and acquitted the other, but the bombmaker’s possible identity remained a mystery for years.Al-Marimi, now in his mid-70s, is charged with two counts of destruction of an aircraft resulting in death. He faces a maximum penalty of life in prison if convicted.Al-Marimi worked for the Libyan intelligence service from approximately 1973-2011, rising to the rank of colonel, according to prosecutors.Prosecutors believe he brought a suitcase containing a bomb to an airport in Malta and gave it to co-conspirators for a flight to Frankfurt, Germany. The suitcase travelled from Frankfurt to London, where it was loaded onto Flight 103, according to investigators.

https://www.politico.eu/article/icc-top-.text: THE HAGUE — The European Commission should act “as soon as possible” to give clear guidance on U.S. sanctions against the International Criminal Court, its top administrative official told POLITICO in an interview. Osvaldo Zavala Giler, who oversees the day-to-day functioning of the Hague-based court as the institution's registrar, said his job became “preparing for sanctions” as the White House imposed an escalating regime of restrictions against it. The Trump administration targeted prosecutors and judges from the court first in February 2025 before announcing blanket sanctions on Oct. 9 this year. The EU has repeatedly backed the Court against Washington , but it has resisted calls to activate a mechanism that would forbid firms from complying with U.S. laws. Advertisement Advertisement That has agonized senior figures in The Hague. Zavala Giler said the Commission's "lack of clarity" left private companies and NGOs in the dark over whether they should comply with sanctions decided by Washington — and what risks they face if they don't. Zavala Giler's call to the Commission adds to pressure from EU lawmakers for a swift response after the Oct. 9 announcement. Kallas told the European Parliament on Tuesday that Brussels would use the next few months "to open dialogue" on the issue. The new sanctions are set to take effect in April next year. "What I would hope is that the space for dialogue is not interpreted as a space for waiting to protect the court," Zavala Giler said, who spoke from his glass office on the eve of a visit to the Court’s headquarters by the EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas. Damocles sword Anticipating sweeping sanctions, the Court spent six months abandoning U.S. tech providers and moving to an open-source software environment, and 20 months to make its financial transactions dollar-proof. That move has been a huge undertaking for Zavala Giler's team, he said. The Court initially deepened its reliance on U.S. technology after it was hit by a massive cyber attack in 2023, but what seemed a solution at that time became a problem in the face of sanctions. Even though the current regime includes a carveout for telecommunications, there is no guarantee it will remain the case. "It becomes a sort of Damocles sword on top of our head that could be revoked at any time," Zavala Giler said. "I cannot count on U.S. tech companies anymore." Advertisement Advertisement U.S. platforms operate as entire ecosystems, offering all-encompassing solutions under a single contract. To do without them, “you need to start creating your own architecture and systems that need to speak to each other,” the registrar said. Financial autonomy was equally hard to achieve. The Court mapped all its suppliers’ transactions to ensure there was no U.S. nexus, meaning that no U.S. person, bank or currency is involved in a payment. “We made all of our staff members have European bank accounts. It was a very detailed process that we had to do, person by person, company by company, making sure that the contracts were in euros,” the registrar said. The Court also went from working with tens of banks to only “a few,” since only a handful of institutions are comfortable with dollar-proof payments. Chilling effect That situation is likely to worsen without clear guidance from EU countries and the Commission. As Zavala Giler put it, “if the International Criminal Court cannot transact in Europe, in euros within the SEPA zone with no U.S. nexus, then there is a bigger question about European financial sovereignty.” The Court has long called the EU to use a legislative shield — known as blocking statute — that would forbid EU firms from complying with U.S. sanctions. The request was backed by dozens of lawmakers at the European Parliament, which incidentally awarded the court its human rights Sakharov Prize on Thursday. The blocking statute “becomes an instrument to reassert the minimum space that should not be affected by unilateral extraterritorial sanctions ... that minimum space should be, at the very least, the eurozone,” Zavala Giler said. Even without it, the court needs “the reassurances that, at least within the eurozone, [it] can continue to operate,” he added. Advertisement Advertisement So far, however, the Commission has taken a cautious approach, choosing dialogue with the U.S. as a way of "buying time," as a EU diplomat put it to POLITICO. In a balancing act, EU heads of state and government backed Brussels' diplomatic effort at their summit last week, while also committing to do whatever is needed to support the Court. “I hope that now that the European Council has opened this door, the Commission will feel more comfortable in taking an extra step. And at the very least, providing some kind of clear guidance,” Zavala Giler said. As an intermediate step, the registrar suggested the use of “comfort letters” reassuring firms that they should not comply with the U.S. measures. Zavala Giler stressed that sanctions were not only a matter to address for banks and tech operators, as the current uncertainty has already affected NGOs working with the Court. NGOs play a critical role in supporting the work of the Court, for instance "to provide reparations for victims in Uganda" or "to assist the work of the court in providing assistance to victims in Ukraine." “This has created an enormous chilling effect," he said. "They don’t know if they have the legal protections or not, to continue supporting the work of the court.” Advertisement Advertisement The registrar's office overlooks the moat circling the court's six towers across the compound's 46,000 square meters. In one of these buildings, the trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte over alleged crimes against humanity is due to begin next month. Reporters who will cover the proceeds won't be allowed to use their phones — only paper and pen. It is Zavala Giler's job to oversee this huge institution, which relies on secure communications, cross-border funding for investigations and the contribution of many NGOs. "This court has for victims the promise of the never again," Zavala Giler said.
